---
title: "Compared with established QDA software"
---


Whether to move a project to a different tool is a decision with real costs.
This page is meant to help you make it, which means it has to be usable
against this ecosystem as well as for it.

## What is being compared

qdaR on its own is a library. Nobody switches to a library. The realistic
comparison is between an established programme — MAXQDA, ATLAS.ti, NVivo, QDA
Miner, Dedoose — and the **combination** of Zotero, the zotQDA plugin for
coding, qdaZ for analysis in a window, and qdaPy or qdaR for analysis in a
script. That combination is what the rest of this page calls *the ecosystem*.

## Monolith or ecosystem

The deepest difference is not a feature list. MAXQDA, ATLAS.ti and NVivo are
**monoliths**: transcription, coding, analysis, statistics and figures in one
programme, from one vendor, with one manual, one file format and one telephone
number. That is a genuine design achievement, and for a great many projects it
is the right answer.

This is a **composed ecosystem**. The work is divided among tools that already
do their part well, and only the joins are new:

| The work | Done by | Standing |
|---|---|---|
| library, documents, metadata, sync | **Zotero** | mature, open source, used by millions |
| transcription and time alignment | **ELAN** | the de-facto standard in language documentation, GPL-3, MPI Nijmegen |
| statistics and figures | **R** and **Python** | the two languages empirical research already runs on |
| coding | zotQDA | new |
| analysis in a window | qdaZ | new |
| the analyses in a script | qdaR, qdaPy | new |

> **The mature parts are borrowed; the young parts are the glue.**

That is the argument in one sentence, and it cuts both ways.

In favour: each job is done by something built for it rather than by one
vendor's version of everything. The pieces outlive the glue — your references,
your transcripts and your analysis scripts survive this project regardless of
what happens to these four plugins. Every seam is an open, documented format,
so you can leave from any of them. And none of it can be withdrawn, priced up
or discontinued.

Against, and these are real costs: **more programs to install and to learn**;
the seams are yours to manage, and a hand-off that a monolith performs
invisibly is a step you take yourself; **nobody is responsible for the whole**,
so when something breaks between two parts there is no single number to call;
and the four new components are young and thinly documented next to a
commercial manual that has had a decade of revisions.

Which way that trade falls depends less on features than on what you already
have. If Zotero, R or ELAN are in your working life anyway, the ecosystem
mostly adds a thin layer. If none of them is, you are adopting four unfamiliar
tools at once to replace one.

### The older idea behind this

The composed-ecosystem argument is not new. It is the Unix one, written down
in 1978 in the foreword to the Bell System Technical Journal's UNIX issue —
McIlroy, Pinson and Tague,
[10.1002/j.1538-7305.1978.tb02135.x](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1978.tb02135.x),
pp. 1899–1904 — as the first two of three maxims:

> (i) Make each program do one thing well. To do a new job, build afresh
> rather than complicate old programs by adding new "features."
>
> (ii) Expect the output of every program to become the input to another, as
> yet unknown, program. Don't clutter output with extraneous information.
> Avoid stringently columnar or binary input formats.

The second maxim is the one that made the first practical, and the mechanism
was the **pipe**: Doug McIlroy's idea, implemented by Ken Thompson in 1973 and
described in Ritchie and Thompson, *The UNIX Time-Sharing System*, CACM 1974,
[10.1145/361011.361061](https://doi.org/10.1145/361011.361061), with the
history told in Ritchie, *The Evolution of the UNIX Time-sharing System*,
1984, [10.1002/j.1538-7305.1984.tb00054.x](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1984.tb00054.x).
Small programs, each good at one job, joined by a plain-text stream, turn out
to do more together than a large program that tries to do everything.

A QDA monolith is the other design. It is not the wrong one — integration buys
real things, and this page names them. But it means that transcription,
coding, statistics and figures are all as good as one vendor decided to make
them, and no better.

Which gives the shortest description of what this project actually is:

> **zotQDA is a pipe operator for qualitative content analysis: it does the
> one thing that was missing — coding, in the reader, on the material where it
> already lives — and connects the tools that could already do the rest.**

That is also why the exchange contract looks the way it does. Nine CSV
formats, each stamping its kind and version into its own first column, plain
text, no binary, nothing clever. It is written for maxim (ii): the output is
expected to become the input of another, as yet unknown, program. qdaR and
qdaPy are two such programs. Yours can be the third.

## How this was checked, and what that is worth

Claims about other programmes come from their own manufacturers'
documentation. The five pages that carry the most weight — the agreement
tooling of MAXQDA, ATLAS.ti, NVivo and QDA Miner, and what MAXQDA Stats
contains — were re-read on **6 August 2026**; the rest come from a survey of
the vendor manuals on **30 July 2026**. Every source is linked at the end.

Three limits worth stating before the tables:

**Feature lists go out of date.** These are commercial products under active
development. A gap named here may have been closed since.

**A missing feature in a manual is weak evidence.** That a manual does not
mention confidence intervals is not proof that the software cannot produce
them. Absence in the documentation is what is claimed, not absence in the
product.

**Universal statements are not provable.** Where this page says something is
not offered *anywhere*, it means: not found in the documentation of the five
programmes surveyed. We searched for sample-size planning in QDA software and
found no such feature documented, which is not the same as knowing there is
none.

## Where the established programmes are ahead

This is the longer list, and it comes first because it decides most cases.

### Audio and video: a division of labour, not a gap

MAXQDA, ATLAS.ti, NVivo and Dedoose code audio and video directly, in the same
window as everything else. The ecosystem splits that work: **ELAN** does the
transcription and time alignment, zotQDA reads the result, and by the time it
reaches this package it is text like any other.

ELAN is an annotation tool for audio and video from The Language Archive at
the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics, open source under GPL-3, in
development for two decades and the de-facto standard in language
documentation, sign-language and gesture research — Wittenburg, Brugman,
Russel, Klassmann and Sloetjes, *ELAN: a Professional Framework for
Multimodality Research*, [LREC 2006](https://aclanthology.org/L06-1082/).

For several purposes it does **more** than the editors built into QDA
packages: an unlimited number of tiers with formal hierarchies, so speech,
translation, gesture and a coding layer sit on one timeline with their
dependencies expressed rather than implied; up to four synchronised video
files; controlled vocabularies that constrain a tier to a defined category
set; and time accuracy as the stated design goal.

Three arguments beyond the features. `.eaf` is documented open XML with a
versioned schema, a CLARIN standard, so the annotation outlives the software
and can be archived, deposited and cited — which a transcript inside a
proprietary project file cannot. ELAN is a described, peer-reviewed research
instrument you can reference in a paper. And it is free, in the sense that
nobody can withdraw it or raise its price.

What the detour costs: a second program with a real learning curve, a manual
hand-off, and no way back — codings made in Zotero do not return to the
timeline. In zotQDA it is stage one of three, so you code a timestamped
transcript with no player, no waveform and no time axis; standalone images are
not covered at all.

**If you code from transcripts, this is a strong combination. If you need to
code while watching the recording, the established tools are ahead.**

**Transcription is not reinvented either.** Nothing here transcribes: that job
goes to Whisper (Radford and colleagues,
[ICML 2023](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/radford23a.html), 680,000 hours
of training audio, weights published) or a comparable model, running locally
so that interview material stays on your machine. WhisperX
([10.21437/Interspeech.2023-78](https://doi.org/10.21437/interspeech.2023-78))
adds word-level timestamps and speaker diarisation, which is what ELAN's tiers
want. A transcription mode written as a side feature of a coding tool is
unlikely to reach that quality — which is the same argument as everywhere else
on this page.

The output is a **draft**, not a transcript. Koenecke and colleagues (FAccT
2024, [10.1145/3630106.3658996](https://doi.org/10.1145/3630106.3658996))
found roughly 1 % of Whisper transcriptions containing entirely fabricated
phrases, 38 % of those carrying explicit harms, and higher rates for speakers
with longer pauses. Accuracy also differs systematically by accent (Graham and
Roll, [10.1121/10.0024876](https://doi.org/10.1121/10.0024876)) and dialect
(Koenecke and colleagues,
[10.1073/pnas.1915768117](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1915768117)), and no
recogniser produces GAT2 or Jefferson conventions. Every automatic transcript
has to be checked against the audio — which is the correction pass ELAN is for.

### Concept maps and networks

MAXQDA has MAXMaps, ATLAS.ti has its network views, both mature and central to
how many people work. The ecosystem has nothing comparable and does not intend
to: this is a stated non-goal, not a gap awaiting a release.

### Statistics without programming

MAXQDA Stats — part of the Analytics Pro licence, not sold separately —
offers descriptive statistics, crosstabs with chi-squared, Phi and Cramér's V,
t-tests, Mann-Whitney U, one-way ANOVA with post-hoc tests, Pearson and
Spearman correlation, and Cronbach's alpha, all in the interface. QDA Miner
with WordStat goes further still, into multidimensional scaling,
correspondence analysis and coding-sequence analysis.

qdaZ deliberately computes no inferential statistics. Everything on this
site's [features page](features.qmd) is real, but reaching it means writing R
or Python. **For a non-programmer, this ecosystem offers less statistics than
MAXQDA Analytics Pro, not more.**

### AI assistance

MAXQDA and ATLAS.ti ship AI summarising and coding suggestions. zotQDA's AI
features are local-only, optional and modest by comparison.

### Maturity, and what comes with it

The commercial products have a support desk, training courses, textbooks, a
decade of published methods papers citing them, and institutional site
licences your library may already pay for. This ecosystem is at version 0.x,
has no user base, no citation record, and no support beyond an issue tracker.
For a dissertation with a deadline, that is a serious argument.

### Collaboration

Dedoose is browser-based and built for several people working at once.
Team work here goes through Zotero group libraries: workable, but sync-based,
with no real-time editing and no built-in access management beyond Zotero's
own.

### One further honest caveat

A zotQDA export has been validated against the official REFI-QDA schemas and
imports of MAXQDA files have been tested against a real study, but the
**reverse round-trip — a zotQDA export opened in MAXQDA — has not yet been
tested on live software**, PDF coordinates in particular. Treat the exit route
as documented rather than demonstrated until that is done.

## Where the ecosystem is ahead

### The reference manager underneath

Every coded fragment carries its citekey, author and year because the material
is a Zotero library, not an imported copy. Crosstabs by collection, year,
author or item tag need no document-variable table, because Zotero already
holds those attributes. In the surveyed programmes, case attributes are
entered and maintained separately.

### Nothing is locked in

Codes are Zotero tags on Zotero annotations; the codebook and the coding log
are notes. All of it is readable, searchable and exportable without the
plugin, and it syncs with everything else in your library. There is no
proprietary project file, and if the plugin disappeared tomorrow your coding
would still be there.

### Agreement statistics

Four of the five surveyed name the coefficients they compute, and **none of
those four documents a confidence interval**. The fifth, QDA Miner, describes
an inter-rater module without saying which coefficients it contains, so
nothing can be claimed about it in either direction. What the manuals say:

| | Coefficients documented |
|---|---|
| MAXQDA | percentage agreement and "Kappa (Rädiker & Kuckartz)" — the manual adds that the chance correction "only makes sense if you include a maximum of 3 codes in the intercoder check" |
| ATLAS.ti | percentage agreement, Holsti index, and the Krippendorff family: alpha binary, cu-alpha, Cu-alpha |
| NVivo | percentage agreement and Cohen's kappa |
| Dedoose | Cohen's kappa, pooled and per code |
| QDA Miner | "a unique inter-rater agreement assessment module"; the public feature page does not name the coefficients |
| this ecosystem | six coefficients, each with a bootstrap confidence interval, plus the paradox diagnostics |

**ATLAS.ti's is the most methodologically ambitious of the commercial tools**,
and its alpha binary addresses the same prior question the unitizing measures
here do. It is the closest competitor on this point by a distance.

### Whether the coders marked the same stretches

Krippendorff's unitizing alpha, WindowDiff, Pk and Mathet's gamma. ATLAS.ti's
alpha binary is the only comparable feature found; the others treat the
segmentation as settled and measure only the categories.

### The coding log as data

zotQDA records every code assignment with a timestamp and a coder. That makes
the coding *process* analysable: activity per day and coder, a saturation
curve over the documents in first-coding order, and coder drift over time. No
surveyed programme exposes its equivalent as an analysable source.

### Planning before there is data

Sample size for a kappa interval (Donner and Rotondi) and for a theme of a
given prevalence (Fugard and Potts). Not found in any surveyed programme.

### Reproducibility

Every qdaZ figure exports as its data plus a Vega-Lite specification, which
qdaR and qdaPy re-render into the same figure. Every coefficient exists in
three independent implementations checked against one frozen reference. A
reviewer asking how a number was produced can be given the file and the code.

### Cost and licence

Free, AGPL-3.0-or-later, with an explicit additional permission placing no
condition on what you produce with it.

## Should you switch?

**Probably yes, if** your material is text you already keep in Zotero, you
report intercoder agreement and want it done properly, you work in R or
Python anyway, reproducibility matters to your field, or a licence is not
affordable.

**Probably not, if** you code audio or video, you need concept maps, you want
statistics without programming, you are on a deadline and need support you can
telephone, several people must code simultaneously, or your institution
already provides a licence and your colleagues use it.

**Worth considering in parallel:** the exchange format works in both
directions. Coding in Zotero and analysing in MAXQDA is possible, as is the
reverse — subject to the untested-round-trip caveat above.

If you find a claim here that is wrong or has gone out of date, please open an
issue. A comparison nobody corrects is a comparison nobody should trust.
